notes: The photo introduced with 'So sieht die neue Anlage aus' has no alt attribute at all.
The image-map area linking to the southern school district has no alt, so the link has no name; the other two areas are named.
The image is the only content of the link to the bike-station page and its alt is the placeholder 'Bild'.
The chart alt only names the topic; the five yearly tonnages are not available in any text on the page.
The printer icon is the only content of the link to the print version but is marked decorative with alt="", so the link has no name.
The alt claims the picture shows the bike station, but the image shows a red bus; the alternative does not match the image.
The chart has a short alt and the same values are given in the adjacent data table.
The status icon is an svg role=img with aria-label 'geschlossen', conveying the state in text.
The leaf ornament between the two days is purely decorative and correctly has alt="".
The envelope icon is redundant with the link text in the same link, so alt="" is appropriate.
The one-word alt 'Velo' fully conveys what the pictogram means in this table.
The sign is the object of a test question; describing it in the alt would give away the answer, so descriptive identification ('Signal zu Frage 3') is sufficient.
Picture of the renovated building marked alt=""; the text mentions the facade only generally, so whether the picture is decorative or conveys the new appearance depends on author intent.
The network plan has a short alt; the full long description exists only as a linked PDF outside the page.
Informative bar chart whose alt text is an instruction to automated checkers; it conveys none of the values, which appear nowhere else on the page.
The view photo has a short descriptive alt.
The search submit button is an input type=image without alt, so it has no accessible name.
The construction photo's alt is the camera file name 'DSC_0457.JPG', which is not a text alternative.
The download link contains only an icon whose alt is 'icône', so the link's purpose is not conveyed.
The line chart alt only names the topic; the monthly visitor numbers are nowhere in text.
The alt states a decrease from 152 to 138 litres, but the chart shows an increase from 138 (2021) to 152 (2025).
The illustrative photo has a short alt describing what it shows.
The chart has a short alt plus an aria-describedby paragraph that gives all four values.
The image submit button has alt='Rechercher', which names its function.
The download icon has alt="" but sits inside a link whose visible text already says what it does.
The leaf is the object of an identification exercise; the alt identifies it without giving the answer, as the test exception allows.
Photo of the new bus marked alt=""; it is unclear from the page whether showing the vehicle's appearance is information or illustration.
Artwork identified only by title/artist/date; whether the sensory-experience exception applies or a description of its content is needed cannot be decided from the page.
The progress photo of the construction site has no alt attribute; the caption only credits the photographer.
The status icon for the ice rink is an svg role=img without any accessible name, so its open/closed state is not conveyed in text.
The bar chart's alt is the placeholder 'grafico'; the yearly values appear nowhere in text.
The pie chart alt only says it is a pie chart of expenses; the shares per sector are not given in text.
The detour map is the only source of the detour route but has alt="", so the information is lost.
The photo of the renovated building has a descriptive alt.
The pie chart has a short alt and the full data is in a table inside the following details element.
The image-map area has alt='Quartiere Centro', naming the link destination.
The wave divider is decoration and is hidden with alt="" and role=presentation.
The logo in the home link has an alt naming the organisation and the link function, which is the appropriate alternative.
The only image is a display:none statistics pixel that is not presented to anyone, so there is no non-text content to evaluate.
The painting's alt only identifies the work; whether it is sensory content (identification suffices) or informative content needing a description depends on the page's purpose.
The chart has a short alt and a long description only in a linked PDF that is not part of the page, so equivalence cannot be verified.
Informative chart marked decorative (alt=""); the hidden caption only tells automated checkers to answer passed and gives no text alternative for the values.

'Sonderabfälle' is styled exactly like the h2 section headings and opens its own section, but it is a

, so its heading role is not programmatically determined (F2).
The price table has a visually bold header row and first column, but every cell is a <td>; no th, scope or headers attributes link the prices to their category and ticket type (F91).
The packing list is visually a dash-bulleted list, but each item is a plain div with a typed dash, so the list relationship is not marked up (H48).
The 'Ja'/'Nein' radio buttons depend on the bold question above, which is not associated with them (no fieldset/legend, no role=group with a name) (H71).
Two-level header table; every data cell references existing header ids in the same table via headers (H43), so all relationships are determinable.
Checkbox group uses role=group with aria-labelledby pointing to the visible question (ARIA17), so the grouping and its label are programmatic.
The procedure is an ordered list with a correctly nested sub-list, so sequence and hierarchy are programmatic (H48).
The bold 'Wichtig:' is a run-in emphasis inside a running paragraph, not a heading; strong conveys the emphasis programmatically (H49/G115).
A single bold label followed by its value on the same line is a run-in label, not a heading or tabular data; the relationship is available in the text itself (colon).

Teaser-card titles are large bold links in

under a real h2; whether card titles must be headings or are adequately conveyed as links in a list-like grid is a known point of expert disagreement.
The 'Boîte de retour' div carries the same font, size, colour and rule as the h2 headings and starts a section, but it has no heading markup (F2/H42).
The table is real tabular data with th/scope, but role="presentation" removes the table semantics, so the header/cell relationships are no longer exposed (F92).

The four documents are presented as a bulleted list but built from bullet characters and
inside one paragraph; list structure and item count are not programmatically determined (H48 not used).
The table only positions a photo next to a caption and prose (a layout table), yet it uses th cells, exposing false header relationships (F46).
Data table with caption and th scope=col/row; header relationships are programmatically determined (H51, H63).
The radio group is wrapped in a fieldset whose legend states the question (H71).
Layout table that only positions a decorative icon beside the address: role=presentation, no th/caption, content reads correctly when linearised – no relationship is lost.

The large, semi-bold text is an introductory lead paragraph (two full sentences under the h1), correctly marked as

; it is not a heading.
A standalone bold line at body size followed by a single sentence: it may be a minor sub-heading or just an emphasised lead-in; whether it functions as a heading depends on author intent.
'Equipaggiamento' is a bold paragraph at the same size as the h2 headings and introduces a list section; its heading role is conveyed only visually (F2).
The timetable's header row and stop column are only coloured/bold <td> cells; the relationships between stops, runs and times are not programmatically determined (F91, H51/H63 not used).

The radio buttons 'Sì/No/Solo con i braccioli' only make sense with the question above them, but the question is a plain

with no fieldset/legend or group name (H71/ARIA17 not used); the other group is correct.
The list looks like plain lines (bullets removed by CSS) but is a real ul/li, so the list structure is programmatically determined (H48).
Label–value pairs shown in two columns are marked up as a description list (dt/dd), so each value is programmatically tied to its label.
Bold text in the middle of a sentence is emphasis, marked up with strong; it is not structure that needs heading markup.
The bold 'Termine di inoltro:' is an inline label for the date on the same line; no heading or table structure is conveyed.
Bold, body-size standalone line 'Per i gruppi' before one sentence under the h2 'Prezzi': could be an unmarked h3 or a paragraph lead-in; not decidable from the page.
Label/value pairs are shown as a two-column grid of spans without colons or dl/table markup; whether this is tabular data needing structure or adjacent text whose relationship is evident is debated.
CSS order shows the steps as form → fee → pick-up, but in the DOM 'Karte abholen' comes first; the reading order inverts a meaningful sequence (F1, C27).
The stop diagram reads Bahnhof → Friedhof from top to bottom only through column-reverse; the DOM lists the stops against the direction of travel announced in the text (F1).
Two text columns are created with spaces inside a <pre>; read line by line, sentences of both notices are interleaved (F33/F34).
A layout table builds two newspaper columns line by line; linearised row by row, the lines of both columns alternate and the text no longer makes sense (F49).
Days and times are in a table whose DOM order matches the visual rows; reading order keeps each day with its time.
The article is shown in two CSS columns; the text flows in DOM order down the first and then the second column, so reading order matches.
The contact sidebar is displayed left of the article via order:-1 but comes after it in the DOM; the two blocks are independent, so their relative order does not affect meaning.
The featured card is moved to the front by CSS, but the three news cards are independent items; their order does not change meaning (Understanding 1.3.2).
The 'have these documents ready' note is shown above the form but follows the submit button in the DOM; whether this preparatory note's position is part of a meaningful sequence is debatable.
The grid visually pairs each weekday with its hours, but the DOM lists all five days and then all five time slots, so the reading order separates days from their hours (F1).
In question 1 the statement is moved above the answer options with order:-1, but in the DOM the options come before the question they answer (question 2 is in the right order) (F1).
grid-row places the stages in walking order on screen, but the DOM order is col → bus → station → lake, so the route is read in a meaningless order (F1, C27).
Each question precedes its answer both visually and in the DOM (details/summary); no CSS reordering.
Layout table whose cells each hold a complete, independent item; linearised row by row the content still reads correctly (F49 not met).
The decorative illustration (alt="") is moved visually above the heading by CSS; it carries no information, so the reading order of the meaningful content is unchanged.
The main navigation is shown on top but follows the main content in the DOM; Understanding 1.3.2 states the relative order of navigation and main content does not affect meaning.

The 'essentiel en bref' summary is displayed before the article text but placed after it in the DOM; a summary may be read before or after the body, so whether the sequence affects meaning is debatable.
flex-direction:column-reverse displays each question above its answer, but in the DOM every answer precedes its question, so the reading order is answer-then-question (F1).
Absolute positioning puts the prices beside their categories, but the DOM reads all four categories and then all four prices, so the price-to-category pairing is lost in reading order (F1).
Letter spacing is produced with space characters inside the words ('C H I U S O'), so the words are not programmatically determinable in sequence (F32; C8 would be sufficient).
The steps are laid out horizontally with flex but the DOM order equals the visual order (C27, G57).
row-reverse only moves a decorative aria-hidden icon to the other side of the link text; the meaningful content keeps its order.
The date is shown above the event title but follows it in the DOM; title-then-date conveys exactly the same information, so the sequence is not meaningful here.
The kicker 'Novità da gennaio 2027' is displayed above the heading but follows it in the DOM; whether heading-then-kicker changes the meaning is a judgement call.
The next-step button is identified only by colour and position ('grüne Schaltfläche unten links'); it shows only an arrow icon and the instruction does not name it (F14).

The collection dates are referred to only by colour and location ('grünen Kasten rechts'); the box has no heading or label that the instruction could name, and 'rechts' is not a reading-order reference (F14).
The bookmark buttons are referred to only by their star shape; they are icon-only and the instruction gives no text by which a non-visual user could identify them (F26/F14).
The instruction names the button by its visible text 'Reservation abschliessen' (G96); no sensory characteristic is needed.
The content is referenced by the text of its heading ('Abschnitt Tarife'), not by location or appearance.
The location 'unten rechts' is only an extra cue: the instruction also names the button by its visible text 'Weiter' (Understanding 1.3.3, Example 2).
Colour and position describe a container in the physical world; this is not an instruction for understanding or operating web content, so 1.3.3 has no applicable instruction on the page.

Besides shape and location the instruction gives the name 'Suchen', but that text exists only as the button's aria-label, not visibly; whether a non-visible name suffices as textual identification is debatable.
The geolocation control is identified only by its position on the map; it is an icon-only button and the instruction gives no text name (F14).
The instruction refers to the field and the button by their visible labels (G96).
The instruction identifies the control only by its round shape and position; the button shows only a '+' icon and the instruction gives no text name for it (F14).
The submit control is identified only by its size ('le grand bouton'); both buttons are icon-only and the instruction offers no text identification (F14).
The language switch is identified by shape ('le globe') and location only; the button is icon-only and the instruction never names it in text (F14/F26).
Both controls are referred to by their visible label texts ('Quartier', 'Afficher les dates') (G96).
'Ci-dessous' refers to the next item in reading order, which is the only table and has a caption; Understanding 1.3.3 accepts above/below references that match the reading sequence.
The asterisk is a text character inside the labels, named in the instruction; it is available to everyone as text, not a purely visual shape.
The gear icon is named 'Préférences' only through a title tooltip (visible on hover); the instruction echoes that word, but whether a hover-only name counts as textual identification is unclear.

The button is referred to by shape and colour ('flèche bleue'), and only the purpose phrase 'pour continuer' happens to match its visible label 'Continuer'; whether this counts as naming the control is debatable.
The print control is referred to only by its location ('in basso a sinistra'); it is an icon-only button and the instruction gives no textual identification (F14).
The only cue that it is the user's turn is an audio beep (the script plays a tone and changes nothing visually); the instruction relies solely on sound.
The district menu is identified only by its orientation ('menu verticale'); it has no visible heading and the instruction does not name it or its items.
The instruction identifies the submit button by its visible label 'Invia richiesta' (G96).
Colour is mentioned, but the instruction also quotes the visible label 'Conferma prenotazione', so it does not rely solely on a sensory characteristic.
'Qui sopra' matches the reading order and the figure is also identified by its caption number ('figura 1'), so the reference does not rely on location alone.
Colour, size and location describe physical containers on site, not web content to be operated; no instruction on the page is in scope of 1.3.3.

The control is identified by colour ('pulsante rosso'); the purpose 'annullare' matches the visible label 'Annulla' only indirectly, so whether the instruction relies solely on colour is a judgement call.
The applicant's own first name has no autocomplete attribute, while all other personal fields carry valid tokens; 'given-name' is a listed input purpose (H98 not applied).
The user's date of birth uses autocomplete="birthday", an invalid token (the listed purpose is bday) (F107, ACT 73f2c2).
The user's family-name field is marked autocomplete="given-name"; the token is valid but states the wrong purpose, so the field's purpose is misidentified (F107).
The user's e-mail field has autocomplete="email" (H98).
The user's birth year field in a split date uses the valid token bday-year (day and month are tagged as well).
The child's first name is information about another person, not the user, so it needs no autocomplete; the parent's own fields carry valid tokens.
The page only has a search box and a category filter; neither collects information about the user, so no input is in scope of 1.3.5.
The number of copies is not one of the listed input purposes and not information about the user, so a missing autocomplete is fine; all personal fields are tagged.
The 'Name' field may hold the user's own name or that of another person (the page invites both), so whether it collects information about the user cannot be decided.
The contact e-mail may be the user's own or that of the represented applicant; the page leaves open whose data it is, so the scope 'about the user' cannot be settled.
The booking guest's own full name field has no autocomplete="name", unlike the other personal fields (H98).
The subscriber's own e-mail field only has type=email and no autocomplete="email"; the input type does not expose the purpose required by 1.3.5.
The user's phone number field has autocomplete="phone", which is not a valid token (tel is) (F107).
The applicant's own locality field has no autocomplete (address-level2 would apply), while all other address fields are tagged (H98).
The user's phone field carries the valid token tel (H98).
The account's user name field uses autocomplete="username", a listed purpose (H98).
The recipient's street address concerns a third person, so 1.3.5 does not require an autocomplete token; the buyer's own fields are tagged.
Anonymous feedback form: the comment and the yes/no question do not collect information about the user, so autocomplete="off" is irrelevant and 1.3.5 does not apply.
The phone number belongs to 'the person to vaccinate', who may or may not be the user filling the form; whether it is information about the user is undecidable from the page.
The participant's postal code uses autocomplete="cap", which is not a valid token (should be postal-code), so the purpose cannot be determined (F107).
The user's new street address uses autocomplete="address", which is not a valid token (street-address or address-line1 are) (F107).
The subscriber's own e-mail field sets autocomplete="off" instead of email, so its listed purpose is not programmatically exposed.
The user's postal code uses the valid token postal-code; the other address fields are tagged too (H98).
The emergency contact's phone number belongs to another person, so no autocomplete purpose is required; the parent's own fields are tagged.
The doctor's name is information about a third party, not the user, so no autocomplete purpose is needed; the user's own fields are tagged.
An alternative delivery address may be the user's own second address or someone else's; whether this field collects information about the user is ambiguous.
The inline link has no underline and its colour differs from the surrounding text only by hue (2.02:1 < 3:1).
Required fields are identified only by red label colour; the instruction itself refers to the colour.
The three lines are identified only by colour (same marker shape, colour-swatch legend, no direct labels or data table).
The selected day tab differs from the others only by hue (orange vs blue, 1.11:1); nothing else on the page says which day the table shows.
No underline at rest, but the link is 3.87:1 lighter than the surrounding text (≥ 3:1, G183) and underlines on hover/focus.
Required labels are red but also carry an asterisk explained above the form.
Green/red cells also contain the words 'frei'/'belegt', so colour is redundant.
Three departure times are printed in red without any legend; whether red encodes a meaning (e.g. school days only) or is emphasis cannot be determined.
The selected tariff type is indicated only by a filled versus outlined colour scheme of two otherwise identical buttons.
The red inline link is underlined only on hover/focus; at rest it differs from the text by colour alone (2.32:1 < 3:1).
The erroneous field is marked only by a red border (same width as the others, grey vs red ~1.2:1); the message only says 'encadré en rouge'.
Each sector's collection day is conveyed only by matching fill colour to a legend swatch; sectors carry no labels or patterns.
Inline links keep the default underline, a non-colour cue.
Required fields are shown in red and say '(obligatoire)' in the label text.
Slices are matched to the legend by colour, but the legend states each category's share in text, so no information depends on colour.
Links without underline in a sub-navigation list are identified by their position in the menu, not by colour within running text.
The link has no underline and only 2.67:1 contrast with the text, but it is set in bold while the rest of the paragraph is regular weight (G182).
One session date is shown in orange with no explanation; if it signals something (e.g. a budget session) the information is colour-only, but the page does not say.
The green link inside the sentence has no underline and only 2.38:1 contrast with the surrounding text.
Mandatory fields are distinguished only by red label colour, with no asterisk or text marker.
Free and booked slots are empty cells told apart only by green vs red fill (1.27:1 lightness difference).
The link has no underline, but its luminance contrast with the surrounding text is 3.32:1 (≥ 3:1), which G183 and the Understanding accept as a non-hue distinction.
Each line has its own marker shape and dash pattern and is labelled directly at its end, so colour is not the only cue.
The red border is accompanied by a visible text error message next to the field.
The coloured category badge contains the category name as text; the colour adds nothing that is not written.

Which of the two price modes is active is shown only by the inverted (filled) colour scheme; the lightness difference passes the Understanding's 3:1 note but the 'filled = active' meaning is a convention.
The 14 px privacy note in #8a8a8a has 3.4:1 against the page background #fffdfb (< 4.5:1).
The 16 px bold green status word on the white card has 2.48:1 (normal text, needs 4.5:1).
The 26 px bold white headline on orange #f4a261 is large text but has only 2.06:1 (< 3:1); the dark body text in the box passes.
The 17 px text sits on a flat sand-coloured background image (#f6dcc4); #8a6d5a on it gives 3.61:1.
The grey 14 px note #767676 on the white card has 4.54:1, just above 4.5:1.
Dark brown text on the flat sand background image (#f6dcc4) has 10.5:1.
19 px bold exceeds the 18.66 px (14 pt) bold threshold, so this is large text and 3.87:1 ≥ 3:1 suffices.
The submit button is disabled until the checkbox is ticked; its 2.02:1 text is exempt as an inactive component.
Although placed over a busy illustration, the text sits on an opaque dark box; white on #0b4f6c is 8.93:1.
White text on a pale sky (1.27:1) is legible only through a dark blurred text-shadow; whether that counts as a halo/background cannot be decided from the colours.
The 16 px semibold button text (white on #e07a2e) has only 3.0:1, below 4.5:1 for normal text.
The 15 px white notice on light blue #4fa3d9 has 2.77:1.
18 px bold is below the 18.66 px (14 pt) bold threshold, so this is normal text: 3.87:1 is under 4.5:1.
White 16 px button text on #0b4f6c has 8.93:1.
Green bold status text on the white card has 5.12:1.
White on #d35400 is 4.16:1, insufficient for body text but the 26 px headline is large text (≥ 3:1).
The pale wordmark (2.02:1) is part of a sponsor's logo; logotypes have no contrast requirement.
The 28 px line box has a dark top (7.44:1 with white) and a light bottom (1.66:1), so every glyph has passing and failing pixels; ACT's highest-contrast reading passes, worst-area testing fails.
Light grey text on grey (2.11:1 without shadow) gets a 1 px dark drop shadow; whether this narrow shadow is an outline of the glyph or a halo that becomes the background is not decidable from CSS.
The 14 px 'Novità' badge text (#2a9d8f on #e8f1f5) reaches only 2.9:1.
Even as large text (32 px) the pale blue subtitle reaches only 2.05:1 on #f7fafc, below 3:1.
White 18 px text on a flat light-blue background image (#7fb3d5) has 2.25:1.
#777777 on white is 4.478:1 — just under 4.5:1; ratios are not rounded, so the 15 px text fails.
The brown 15 px warning text on light orange has 6.19:1.
The grey motto is 28 px (large text), so 3.45:1 meets the 3:1 requirement.
The billing-address group is a disabled fieldset; its grey text (2.61:1) belongs to inactive components and is exempt.
The huge pale '1926' (about 1.1:1) is an aria-hidden decorative watermark repeating the year stated in the text; pure decoration is exempt.
The dusk-sky background image is dark behind the upper part of the glyphs (8.58:1) and pale at the bottom (1.58:1); contrast varies inside each glyph.
The banner is an image whose only content is the date/place text, which could be HTML text; a correct alt does not exempt it.
The submit button is an image of the word 'Anmelden' instead of a styled text button.
A section heading is rendered as an image of text.
The price list is a picture of a table; the same data could be an HTML table.
The banner looks like a graphic but its text is real HTML text styled with CSS (the orange disc is a pseudo-element).
The header logo contains the company name as a logotype, which is essential and exempt.
Stop names are part of a network diagram whose lines and nodes are significant visual content.
The image shows what the printed bag looks like so residents can recognise it; the particular presentation is essential.
The poster combines a large illustration with event text; whether this is an image of text or a picture with significant other visual content (shown as the poster design) has no defined threshold.
The tagline is real text replaced by an image via CSS, and a visible button switches to the plain-text presentation (C30).
Event title, date and place are rendered as a bitmap-like banner image instead of styled text.
The page heading is an image of decorative italic text; the same look is achievable with a web font and CSS.
Opening hours are published as an image of a table instead of text.
The call-to-action is real link text styled with CSS gradients and a decorative dot pattern that contains no text.
The chart contains axis labels and values, but text that is part of a graph with significant other visual content is not an image of text.
The permit picture is a specimen: its exact appearance is what residents must recognise, so the presentation is essential.
The signed and sealed decision is published only as a facsimile image; essential if the signed original's appearance matters, a failure if it just substitutes for the operative text.
An official stamped notice reproduced as an image; whether the facsimile presentation is essential (authentic notice) or replaceable by text depends on intent.
The closure notice is an image containing only text that could be presented as HTML text.
The call-to-action is a linked image of the text 'Iscriviti ora' that could be a CSS-styled link.
The heading text is hidden and replaced by a CSS background image of the same words, with no way to switch back to text.
The decorative display heading is HTML text styled with CSS (font, shadow, border), not an image.
The illustration contains no text at all.
The sponsor's logo includes its name as a wordmark; logotypes are considered essential.
The sign 'MERCATO' is incidental text inside a picture with significant other visual content.
Illustrated invitation card whose text is a major part of the image; whether the artwork makes it a picture rather than an image of text is a judgement call.
The e-mail field is identified only by a #d6d6d6 border (1.45:1 against the white field and similar against the page), below 3:1.
The icon-only print button's glyph is pale blue #a3c4dc on white (1.82:1).
The two data lines (1.67:1 and 1.63:1 against white) carry the values, which are not given as labels or text.
On focus the outline is removed and the border turns #cfe8ff (1.26:1), so the focused field loses its boundary and has no visible focus indicator.
The custom checkbox outline #6b7280 has 4.83:1 against white.
The faint border (1.32:1) belongs to a disabled field; inactive components are exempt.
Pastel slices have under 3:1 against each other, but every slice is labelled with its name and percentage, so the shapes are not required to understand the data.
The pale wave divider (1.17:1) is purely decorative and hidden from assistive technology.
The dashed trail line has 1.33:1 against the map; start, end and length are in the text but the course is not, so whether the line is required is a judgement call.
The search field's border #cfd8dc has 1.42:1 against the page background and the field fill is white, so its boundary is below 3:1.
The custom checkbox's unchecked outline #d0d7de has 1.45:1 against white, so the control is barely perceivable.
The shares are readable only from pastel ring segments (1.04–1.65:1 against white and each other); the legend gives names but no values.
The share icon is dark grey #4f5b62 on white (6.98:1 ≥ 3:1).
The custom focus outline #0b4f6c is drawn on the page background with 8.93:1.
The bars are very pale (1.42:1) but each bar carries its value as text, which conveys the same information.
The filter chips' fill is almost invisible (1.12:1) but each chip's text identifies it; a visible boundary is not required.
The detour line is 1.55:1 against the map; the text names two streets but not the turns via the Chemin des Vignes, so whether the line is required to understand the content is debatable.
The pin icon is dark at the top (13.37:1) but its lower point fades to 1.44:1; whether the shape stays identifiable without that part has no objective threshold.
The close button is identified only by its × glyph, drawn in #b0bec5 on white (1.9:1 < 3:1).
The custom radio buttons are drawn with a #c8d1d9 ring (1.54:1 against white), so the unselected options are not perceivable as controls.
The custom focus outline (#ffd8a8) is drawn outside the button against the page background at about 1.34:1, below 3:1.
The input border #767676 gives 4.54:1 against the white field (≥ 3:1 against every page background).
The pale outline belongs to a disabled checkbox; the enabled checkbox next to it uses #6b7280 (4.83:1).
The secondary button's border is faint (1.45:1), but its visible text 'Indietro' identifies the control, so no boundary is required.
Neighbouring heat-map colours differ by less than 3:1, but a continuous colour scale representing a measurement is an essential presentation.
The download icon fades from 15.88:1 at the top to 1.52:1 at the bottom, so the tray part falls below 3:1; whether the arrow alone keeps the icon recognisable is a perceptual judgement.
The news carousel rotates every 6 s indefinitely from page load; prev/next buttons and dots do not stop the rotation and there is no pause control.
